title: Let me introduce my friend
goal: Introduce other people, tell informal and formal address apart right down to the verb form, and say what people do for a living.
bekal: introduce a third person to the person you're talking to
switch from *tu* to *Lei* when the situation calls for it
state a job without an article

dialogs.title: Dialogo — In corridoio
dialogs.intro: Giulia runs into Budi in the hallway along with one of the professors. Notice how her way of speaking changes depending on whom she is talking to.

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Budi, ti presento Marco. È il mio amico.

lines.literal: Budi, to-you I-introduce Marco. is the friend my.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Nice to meet you, Marco. I'm Budi.

lines.speaker: Marco:
lines.text: Piacere! Sei uno studente del corso?

lines.text: Sono cuoco. Lavoro in un ristorante qui vicino.

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.id: Good morning, Professor! May I introduce Budi?

lines.text: Buongiorno. Piacere. Lei come si chiama?

lines.text: Molto bene. Ci vediamo in aula, allora.

notes: **Lei is not "she" here.** Italian shows respect by using the third-person feminine form, written with a capital letter: *Lei come si chiama?* is literally "how does she call herself?" — and it's used for men and women alike. It feels odd at first, but this is how Italian keeps a polite distance.
**So the verb moves too.** *Come stai?* (informal) becomes *Come sta?* (formal). *Che lavoro fai?* becomes *Che lavoro fa?*. The form used is the *lui/lei* form, not the *tu* form.

**When to switch to Lei.** With older people, officials, doctors, shop owners, and anyone you don't know who seems senior to you. Only drop to the informal form when the other person offers (*diamoci del tu* = let's just use *tu*). Italians rarely take offense because you were too polite, but often do for the opposite.

**Jobs without an article.** *Sono cuoco*, not *sono un cuoco*. That's different from English, which needs *a*. The article only appears when the job is described: *sono un cuoco bravo* (I'm a good cook).
**Ti presento vs Le presento.** *Ti* = to you, *Le* = to you (formal). These little pronouns go **before** the verb, unlike English, which puts them after.
**Che lavoro fai** literally means "what work do you do". The alternatives are *Che cosa fai?* or, in full, *Che cosa fai nella vita?* — "what do you do in life". All three are common.
**Ci vediamo** = "see you", literally "we see each other". It's one of the goodbyes Italians use most every day, alongside *ciao* and *a presto*.

**Allora** is an all-purpose linking word: "then", "so", "well then". It also fills pauses while you think, like "so…" or "well…". You don't have to use it, but you do have to recognize it — Italians sprinkle it everywhere.

grammars.title: Two registers — informal and formal
body: Compare the left and right columns. It's not only the pronoun that changes, but the verb form too.
after: The formal form uses the *lui/lei* row — exactly the same form as "he/she". So every time you learn the "he/she" form, you've learned the polite form too. Two for the price of one.
Writing *Lei* with a capital L is a habit of formal writing. In conversation you obviously can't see it, but it's kept in emails and letters.

grammars.title: Fare — the verb "to do, to make"
body: The second verb you must learn by heart. It's irregular and shows up everywhere: asking about jobs, the weather, making things.
after: You can state a job two ways: *sono ingegnere* (no article) or *faccio l'ingegnere* (with an article, because here the job is the object). Both are common; the first is slightly more neutral.

blocks.text: Most job titles change form to match the person's gender. Those ending in **-e** usually don't change at all.

*Dottore* and *dottoressa* are used far more widely than the English "doctor": anyone with a university degree can be addressed this way, and in government offices it's almost automatic. The short form before a name: *dottor Rossi*.

blocks.title: Asking about jobs
items: Formal: *Che lavoro fa?* / *Che cosa fa nella vita?*
Not working yet: *Studio ancora.* (I'm still studying) or *Sono disoccupato.*
